Likelihood ratios for forensic comparisons, how well a system that reports them is calibrated, and the plots that show it.

Each section is one help page: what the function is for, the example of its
help page as it runs, and the plot of its result where the package draws
one. `?name` gives the arguments and the value in full.

## Genotype match probability

`gtmp()`: The chance that an unrelated person from the same population shares a DNA profile, locus by locus and overall. With `theta = 0` this is the product rule (`p^2` for a homozygote, 2pq for a heterozygote). A positive `theta` applies the Balding-Nichols correction for shared ancestry. That never makes a homozygote match rarer than the product rule says; it can make a heterozygote match rarer when both alleles are common. See `proof("gtmp")`.

```{r gtmp}
gtmp(p = c(D3 = 0.1, vWA = 0.2), q = c(0.3, NA), hom = c(FALSE, TRUE),
     theta = 0.03)
```

## Posterior probability from a likelihood ratio

`lrpost()`: Turns a likelihood ratio into the probability of the first hypothesis, which needs a prior. A large ratio with a small prior can still leave that probability low; reading the ratio as the probability is the prosecutor's fallacy. See `proof("lrpost")`.

```{r lrpost}
lrpost(lr = 1e6, prior = 1 / 5e6)
```

## Log-likelihood-ratio cost

`cllr()`: Scores a set of likelihood ratios against the truth. Ratios from same-source comparisons should be large and ratios from different-source comparisons small. The cost is 1 for a system that always answers 1. It is above 0 for any set of ratios, and tends to 0 as the ratios of a system that separates the two kinds perfectly grow without bound. See `proof("cllr")` and `cllrmin()`.

```{r cllr}
cllr(same = c(50, 200, 8), diff = c(0.01, 0.2, 1.5))
```

## Log-likelihood-ratio cost after recalibration

`cllrmin()`: Splits the cost of a set of likelihood ratios into `min`, their cost after recalibration with the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm, which keeps their order and gives each block of pooled ratios the value that costs that block least, and `cal`, the rest (`cllr - min`). That `min` is the least cost of every order-keeping recalibration, so that `cal` is never negative, is not proved. A system can separate the two kinds of comparison well and still report ratios that are too large or too small. See `proof("cllrmin")` and `proof("lrcal")`.

```{r cllrmin}
cllrmin(same = c(50, 200, 8), diff = c(0.01, 0.2, 1.5))
```

## Calibrated likelihood ratios

`lrcal()`: Recalibrates a set of likelihood ratios against the truth with the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm, keeping their order. The result can hold 0 and `Inf`: the data never contradicted those ratios. See `proof("lrcal")`.

```{r lrcal}
lrcal(same = c(50, 200, 8), diff = c(0.01, 0.2, 1.5))
```

## Tippett plot

`tipplt()`: For each value on the axis, the share of same-source and of different-source likelihood ratios above it. A good system keeps the same-source curve high to the right of 0 and the different-source curve low; where each crosses 0 shows the rate of misleading evidence. `proof()` records no theorem for this plot.

```{r tipplt}
tipplt(same = c(50, 200, 8, 0.5), diff = c(0.01, 0.2, 1.5, 0.001))
```

## Empirical cross-entropy plot

`eceplt()`: The information a set of likelihood ratios still leaves missing, across prior odds: for the ratios as reported, for the same ratios after calibration, and for a system that always reports 1. Reported ratios above the last curve do harm at that prior. At even prior odds the first two curves pass through the values of `cllrmin()`. `proof()` records no theorem for this plot.

```{r eceplt}
eceplt(same = c(50, 200, 8, 0.5), diff = c(0.01, 0.2, 1.5, 0.001))
```

## Mixture likelihood ratio

`mixlr()`: The weight of a DNA mixture at one locus for one account of who contributed against another. Each account names the alleles of the mixture its known contributors do not explain and the number of unknown contributors who must explain them. Peak heights, drop-out and coancestry are not modelled. See `proof("mixlr")`.

```{r mixlr}
# victim explains a and b; suspect would explain c and d
p <- c(a = 0.1, b = 0.2, c = 0.05, d = 0.15)
mixlr(p, np = character(0), xp = 0, nd = c("c", "d"), xd = 1)
```

## Continuous DNA mixture likelihood ratio (gamma model)

`gmixlr()`: The weight of a DNA mixture for one account of who contributed against another, from the peak heights, not only from which alleles were seen. Each account names the reference profiles it holds to be contributors (`hp`, the prosecution's, usually the person of interest and any undisputed contributor; `hd`, the defence's); the rest of the `nc` contributors are unknown people whose genotypes are summed over. The model's parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood under each account separately and the ratio of the two maxima reported, marker by marker and over all markers.

```{r gmixlr}
# a two-person mixture at two markers: is S a contributor, with the
# victim V, or are V and an unknown person?
peaks <- data.frame(locus = rep(c("D3", "vWA"), c(4, 3)),
                    allele = c(14, 15, 16, 17, 16, 17, 18),
                    height = c(1210, 380, 1150, 420, 1400, 1960, 610))
freq <- data.frame(locus = rep(c("D3", "vWA"), c(5, 5)),
                   allele = c(13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19),
                   freq = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.25, 0.2,
                            0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1))
ref <- data.frame(id = rep(c("V", "S"), each = 2),
                  locus = rep(c("D3", "vWA"), 2),
                  a1 = c(14, 16, 15, 17), a2 = c(16, 17, 17, 18))
gmixlr(peaks, freq, ref, hp = c("V", "S"), nc = 2, hd = "V")
```

```{r gmixlr-plot}
res <- gmixlr(peaks, freq, ref, hp = c("V", "S"), nc = 2, hd = "V")
plot(res)
```

## Kinship index

`kinidx()`: The weight of two DNA profiles for a stated relationship against no relationship, locus by locus and overall. Loci are taken as independent; there is no allowance for mutation or coancestry. See `proof("kinidx")`.

```{r kinidx}
kinidx(g1 = c(12, 14), g2 = c(12, 14), freq = c(0.1, 0.2), rel = "sibling")
```

## Paternity index

`patidx()`: The weight of the DNA evidence that an alleged father is the father of a child, against an unrelated man, locus by locus and overall. With the mother's genotype the index uses the allele the child must have received from the father; without it the index is the parent-child `kinidx()`. There is no allowance for mutation, so one inconsistent locus gives an index of 0. See `proof("patidx")`.

```{r patidx}
patidx(child = c(12, 14), father = c(14, 15), freq = c(0.1, 0.2),
       mother = c(12, 12))
```

## Pedigree likelihood ratio

`pedlr()`: The weight of DNA profiles for one family tree against another: is this child the son of that man, are these remains the missing brother of the people who reported him missing, are two people full or half siblings. Each tree is a table of people and their parents; people who are not typed (a dead parent, a missing relative) are summed over. The likelihood of the profiles is computed under each tree, marker by marker, and the ratio reported with its base-10 logarithm, the product over independent markers.

```{r pedlr}
# is AF the father of C? The mother M is typed too.
trio <- data.frame(id = c("AF", "M", "C"), fid = c(NA, NA, "AF"),
                   mid = c(NA, NA, "M"))
alt <- data.frame(id = c("AF", "M", "C", "X"), fid = c(NA, NA, "X", NA),
                  mid = c(NA, NA, "M", NA))
geno <- data.frame(id = rep(c("AF", "M", "C"), 2),
                   locus = rep(c("D3", "vWA"), each = 3),
                   a1 = c(14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 17),
                   a2 = c(16, 17, 16, 18, 17, 19))
freq <- data.frame(locus = rep(c("D3", "vWA"), c(4, 4)),
                   allele = c(14, 15, 16, 17, 16, 17, 18, 19),
                   freq = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.25, 0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1))
pedlr(trio, geno, freq, alt)
# the child's vWA allele 19 cannot come from AF without a mutation
pedlr(trio, geno, freq, alt, mut = "equal", rate = 0.002)
```

```{r pedlr-plot}
res <- pedlr(trio, geno, freq, alt, mut = "equal", rate = 0.002)
plot(res)
```

## Database search

`dbsrch()`: What a match found by trawling a database is worth. `np` is the bound of the second National Research Council report: the match probability times the number of profiles searched. `any` is the exact chance of at least one chance match among that many unrelated profiles, never above `np`. `post` takes the other view (Balding and Donnelly): everyone else in the database was excluded, so among `pop` possible sources with equal prior the matching person's probability of being the source goes up, not down. See `proof("dbsrch")`.

```{r dbsrch}
dbsrch(mp = 1e-9, n = 5e6, pop = 3e7)
```

## Likelihood ratio of measured evidence

`preslr()`: Weighs measurements (a tissue density, a pXRF calcium level, a marker of antemortem ingestion) under two competing hypotheses, each a normal model of what the measurement would be: the likelihood ratio is the probability of the evidence under H1 over that under H2. Its verbal band follows the usual forensic scale on |log10 LR|: 0 none, up to 1 weak, 2 moderate, 3 moderately strong, 4 strong, 6 very strong, above extremely strong support. The ratio measures support, not the probability that a hypothesis is true.

```{r preslr}
preslr(c(1.9, 2.3, 2.1), m1 = 2, s1 = 0.3, m2 = 1, s2 = 0.4)
```

## Two-level model for multivariate trace evidence

`tlvc()`, `tlvlr()`: `tlvc()` estimates the background of the two-level normal model of Aitken and Lucy (2004) from a reference collection, `x_ij = theta_i + e_ij`, items `theta_i ~ N(mu, C)` and measurements within an item `e_ij ~ N(0, U)`: the overall mean, the pooled within-item covariance and the ANOVA between-item covariance (unbiased for any pattern of replication). `tlvlr()` gives the likelihood ratio of same source against different sources for two items (a control and a recovered fragment, say) from their mean vectors, computed in logarithms from Cholesky factors so that atypical or distant items give a finite value.

```{r tlvc}
set.seed(1)
th <- matrix(rnorm(20, 10, 2), 10, 2)
x <- th[rep(1:10, each = 3), ] + matrix(rnorm(60, 0, 0.2), 30, 2)
bg <- tlvc(x, rep(1:10, each = 3))
tlvlr(th[1, ], th[1, ] + 0.05, 3, 3, bg)
tlvlr(th[1, ], th[2, ], 3, 3, bg)
```

## Scott-Knott grouping of measurements

`skp()`: Splits sorted measurements into groups that differ (Scott and Knott 1974) when the variance of one measurement is known, as in the forensic glass version of Triggs, Curran, Buckleton and Walsh (1997): a segment is split at the cut with the largest between-groups sum of squares when that is significant at `alpha`, judged against `nsim` simulated samples of independent normal values with the known variance (a test of exact size under that null).

```{r skp}
set.seed(1)
x <- c(rnorm(5, 1.5180, 4e-5), rnorm(5, 1.5195, 4e-5))
skp(x, s2 = 4e-5^2, nsim = 199, seed = 1)
```

## Glass fragments recovered under transfer and persistence

`tfrp()`: The probability of recovering 0, 1, ... fragments of glass from a suspect under the transfer, persistence and recovery model of Curran, Triggs, Buckleton, Walsh and Hicks (1998), with uncertain parameters averaged over: the transfer amount and the distance deterministically (by quadrature), the time since the offence exactly, and the loss and recovery rates by `nsim` Monte Carlo draws (exactly when every rate is fixed).

```{r tfrp}
par <- c(80, 50, 0.5, 0.05, 0.8, 0.9, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.05, 0.1,
         0.5, 0.7, 1, 1, 0.5)
tfrp(par, ymax = 10, nsim = 100, seed = 1)$prob
```

## Lowess smoothing

`lwss()`: Robust locally weighted regression (Cleveland 1979) with the conventions of the classic implementation, so that the fit equals that of `stats::lowess()`; the fitted values come back in the order of the input, not sorted.

```{r lwss}
lwss(c(3, 1, 2, 5, 4), c(2, 1, 3, 6, 4))
```

## The Chumbley score for two tool-mark profiles

`chmb()`: Compares two striated tool-mark profiles by the deterministic Chumbley score (Chumbley et al. 2010; Hadler and Morris 2018): each profile is trimmed and detrended by its lowess smooth, the pair of windows of `wopt` points with the largest correlation fixes the shift, and windows of `wval` points at that shift are compared with windows at other shifts by a standardised Wilcoxon rank-sum statistic.

```{r chmb}
set.seed(1)
m <- cumsum(rnorm(700))
a <- m[1:600] + rnorm(600, sd = 0.2)
b <- m[51:650] + rnorm(600, sd = 0.2)
chmb(a, b, wopt = 120, wval = 30)
```

## Congruent matching profile segments (CMPS) of two bullet signatures

`cmpsc()`: How many pieces of one land engraved area's signature line up, at one common shift, with another's: the CMPS score of Chen et al. (2019), the count of congruent matching profile segments, with its share of the segments. A high score points to the same barrel, a low one to different barrels; no threshold is implied, since the scores of same- and different-source pairs depend on the data and the settings (Ju and Hofmann 2022).

```{r cmpsc}
set.seed(1)
a <- cumsum(rnorm(600, sd = 0.5)) + sin(seq_len(600) / 9)
b <- a[31:600] + rnorm(570, sd = 0.1)
cmpsc(a, b)
cmpsc(a, cumsum(rnorm(570, sd = 0.5)))$score
```

```{r cmpsc-plot}
res <- cmpsc(a, b)
plot(res)
```
